units.title: The Parts of Speech
units.blurb: The eight jobs a word can do: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection, and how to tell which job a word is doing.

units.title: Subjects, Predicates and Complements
units.blurb: The subject and the predicate, the verb, the four kinds of sentences, and the words that complete a verb: direct and indirect objects, predicate nouns and adjectives, and object complements.

units.title: Phrases and Clauses
units.blurb: Prepositional phrases, appositives, participles, gerunds and infinitives; independent and dependent clauses; and adjective, adverb and noun clauses.

units.title: Sentence Structure
units.blurb: Simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences.

units.title: Diagramming Sentences
units.blurb: The Reed–Kellogg diagram: a picture of a sentence that puts every word where its job belongs. Build diagrams by hand, from subject and verb to noun clauses.

topics.title: The Eight Parts of Speech
topics.short: A word’s part of speech names the job it does in a sentence: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction or interjection.
topics.trouble: Learners memorize a list of words for each part of speech, but the same word can do different jobs: run is a verb in “We run” and a noun in “a long run.”

topics.title: Kinds of Nouns
topics.short: Nouns can be common or proper, concrete or abstract, singular or plural, and collective (team, flock).
topics.trouble: Learners don’t count abstract nouns (courage, idea, friendship) as nouns because you can’t see or touch them.

topics.title: Personal and Possessive Pronouns
topics.short: Personal pronouns change for person (I, you, he), number (I, we) and case (I, me, my). Possessive pronouns show ownership: mine, yours, hers.
topics.trouble: Learners are puzzled when one book calls my and your pronouns and another calls them adjectives or determiners. Grammars label them differently; what matters is that they show ownership and come before a noun.

topics.title: Other Kinds of Pronouns
topics.short: Reflexive and intensive (myself), demonstrative (this, those), indefinite (someone, all), interrogative (who? which?) and relative (who, which, that) pronouns.
topics.trouble: Learners mix up reflexive and intensive uses (“I hurt myself” vs. “I myself built it”), and call this a pronoun even in “this book,” where it describes the noun.

topics.title: Action and Linking Verbs
topics.short: An action verb shows an action. A linking verb (is, seems, becomes, feels) links the subject to a word that renames or describes it.
topics.trouble: Learners think every verb is an action and miss is and seems; or they call feel and look linking verbs even when they show action (“She felt the fabric.”). Test: can you swap in is?

topics.title: Helping Verbs and Verb Phrases
topics.short: Helping verbs (forms of be, have and do, and modals like can, will, should and might) come before the main verb to make a verb phrase.
topics.trouble: Learners mark only the last word as the verb (in “has been running,” only running), or count not and n’t as part of the verb (they are adverbs).

topics.title: Adjectives and Articles
topics.short: Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns: which one, what kind, how many. A, an and the are a special kind called articles.
topics.trouble: Learners miss adjectives that come after a linking verb (“The soup is hot.”) and forget that a, an and the count too.

topics.title: Adverbs
topics.short: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs. They tell how, when, where, how often and how much.
topics.trouble: Learners think every adverb ends in -ly, so they miss very, often, soon and not, and call friendly and lovely (adjectives) adverbs.

topics.title: Prepositions
topics.short: A preposition shows how a noun or pronoun, its object, relates to another word: in the box, after lunch, with Sam.
topics.trouble: Learners call up or down a preposition even when no object follows (“She looked up.”); then it is an adverb.

topics.title: Conjunctions
topics.short: Coordinating conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) join equals; subordinating ones (because, although, when, if) start a dependent clause; correlative pairs (either…or) work together.
topics.trouble: Learners treat because and although like and and but. And after, before and since can be prepositions (after lunch) or conjunctions (after we ate), depending on what follows.

topics.title: Interjections
topics.short: An interjection shows feeling and stands apart from the rest of the sentence: Wow! Oh, I see. Well, maybe.
topics.trouble: Learners think an interjection always needs an exclamation point. A mild one is set off with a comma.

topics.title: One Word, Different Jobs
topics.short: Decide a word’s part of speech by the job it does in this sentence, not by the word alone.
topics.trouble: Learners choose the first part of speech the dictionary lists, instead of checking the word’s job here: light is a noun, a verb or an adjective in different sentences.

topics.title: Complete Subject and Predicate
topics.short: Every sentence splits in two: the complete subject (who or what it is about) and the complete predicate (what is said about it).
topics.trouble: Learners think the subject is always the first word, or always a person.

topics.title: Simple Subject and Verb
topics.short: The simple subject is the key noun or pronoun in the subject. The simple predicate is the verb, with any helping verbs.
topics.trouble: Learners pick a noun inside a prepositional phrase as the subject (in “One of the dogs barks,” the subject is One, not dogs). That mistake causes agreement errors later.

topics.title: Hard-to-Find Subjects
topics.short: Find the subject in questions, in sentences that start with there or here, and in commands, where it is “you,” understood.
topics.trouble: Learners call there or here the subject, and say a command like “Sit down.” has no subject.

topics.title: Four Kinds of Sentences
topics.short: Declarative sentences state, interrogative sentences ask, imperative sentences command, and exclamatory sentences exclaim.
topics.trouble: Learners judge by the end mark alone. “Close the door!” is imperative even with an exclamation point.

topics.title: Compound Subjects and Verbs
topics.short: Two or more subjects can share one verb (“Ana and Leo sang”), and two or more verbs can share one subject (“Leo sang and danced”).
topics.trouble: Learners mistake a compound verb for two sentences and put a comma before the and (“She ran, and jumped.”).

topics.title: Direct Objects
topics.short: A direct object receives the action of the verb. It answers whom? or what? after an action verb: “Mia kicked the ball.”
topics.trouble: Learners call any noun after the verb a direct object, including a predicate noun after a linking verb and the object of a preposition.

topics.title: Indirect Objects
topics.short: An indirect object tells to whom or for whom the action is done: “She gave Sam the map.” It comes between the verb and the direct object.
topics.trouble: Learners swap the two objects. The indirect object comes first and has no to or for in front of it; “She gave the map to Sam” has no indirect object.

topics.title: Predicate Nouns and Predicate Adjectives
topics.short: After a linking verb, a predicate noun renames the subject (“Ana became captain”) and a predicate adjective describes it (“Ana is tall”).
topics.trouble: Learners call a predicate noun a direct object. In “Ana became captain,” captain is Ana, so it renames her; nothing receives an action.

topics.title: Object Complements
topics.short: An object complement follows a direct object and renames or describes it: “They named the puppy Biscuit.” “The news made Dad happy.”
topics.trouble: Learners read “named the puppy Biscuit” as an indirect object and a direct object. But Biscuit is the puppy: it completes the object, so it is an object complement.

topics.title: Prepositional Phrases as Modifiers
topics.short: A prepositional phrase works as an adjective (“the girl with the kite”) or as an adverb (“ran to the park”).
topics.trouble: Learners can’t tell which word the phrase modifies. Ask which word it tells more about: a noun (adjective phrase) or a verb, adjective or adverb (adverb phrase).

topics.title: Appositives
topics.short: An appositive is a noun or noun phrase that renames the noun beside it: “My aunt, a pilot, flew us home.”
topics.trouble: Learners leave out the commas around an appositive that only adds information, or add commas around one that tells which person or thing is meant (“my friend Ana,” when you have many friends).

topics.title: Phrases and Clauses
topics.short: A clause has its own subject and verb. A phrase is a group of words without both.
topics.trouble: Learners think any long group of words is a clause, or that a clause must be a whole sentence.

topics.title: Independent and Dependent Clauses
topics.short: An independent clause can stand alone as a sentence. A dependent clause begins with a word like because, when or which and can’t stand alone.
topics.trouble: Learners write a dependent clause as if it were a sentence (“Because it rained.”).

topics.title: Participles and Participial Phrases
topics.short: A participle is a verb form used as an adjective: “the barking dog,” “the broken vase,” “Waving her hat, Mia ran.”
topics.trouble: Learners call every -ing word a verb. In “the barking dog,” barking describes the dog, so it works as an adjective.

topics.title: Gerunds
topics.short: A gerund is an -ing verb form used as a noun: “Swimming is fun.” “She loves baking bread.”
topics.trouble: Learners can’t tell a gerund from a participle. Ask whether the -ing word names an activity (a noun: gerund) or describes a noun (an adjective: participle).

topics.title: Infinitives
topics.short: An infinitive is to plus a verb. It can work as a noun (“To win was her goal”), an adjective (“a book to read”) or an adverb (“came to help”).
topics.trouble: Learners mix up infinitives and prepositional phrases: “to the store” is a prepositional phrase; “to run” is an infinitive.

topics.title: Adjective Clauses
topics.short: An adjective clause (a relative clause) usually starts with who, whom, whose, which or that, and modifies a noun: “the book that you lent me.”
topics.trouble: Learners end the clause too early, or attach it to the wrong noun. It follows the noun it modifies.

topics.title: Adverb Clauses
topics.short: An adverb clause starts with a subordinating conjunction (because, when, although, if) and tells when, why, how or under what condition.
topics.trouble: Learners think the dependent clause has to come second. It can come first; then a comma usually follows it.

topics.title: Noun Clauses
topics.short: A noun clause does a noun’s job, as a subject or an object: “What you said surprised me.” “I know that she left.”
topics.trouble: Learners call a noun clause an adjective clause because both can start with that or who. Test: a noun clause can be replaced by it or something.

topics.title: Simple and Compound Sentences
topics.short: A simple sentence has one independent clause. A compound sentence joins two or more, with a comma and a coordinating conjunction or with a semicolon.
topics.trouble: Learners call a sentence with a compound verb a compound sentence. “Leo sang and danced” is simple: one subject, one clause.

topics.title: Complex Sentences
topics.short: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.
topics.trouble: Learners think complex means long or hard. “When it rained, we left” is short and complex.

topics.title: Compound-Complex Sentences
topics.short: A compound-complex sentence has two or more independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.
topics.trouble: Learners miscount clauses when a dependent clause sits inside an independent one, or forget that a compound verb is still one clause.

topics.title: Diagrams: Subject and Verb
topics.short: In a Reed–Kellogg diagram, the subject and the verb sit on a baseline, split by a short line that crosses it.
topics.trouble: Learners copy the words in sentence order instead of placing each word by its job, and put helping verbs off the baseline.

topics.title: Diagrams: Adjectives and Adverbs
topics.short: Adjectives and adverbs go on slanted lines under the word they modify.
topics.trouble: Learners hang an adverb that modifies an adjective (very in “very tall”) under the noun instead of under the adjective.

topics.title: Diagrams: Direct and Indirect Objects
topics.short: A direct object follows a short upright line that stops at the baseline. An indirect object sits on a flat line hung under the verb.
topics.trouble: Learners draw the line before a direct object all the way through the baseline, which is the mark for the subject.

topics.title: Diagrams: Complements
topics.short: A predicate noun or adjective follows a line slanted back toward the subject. An object complement follows a line slanted back toward the direct object.
topics.trouble: Learners use the direct-object line for a predicate noun. The slant points back to the word it renames or describes.

topics.title: Diagrams: Prepositional Phrases
topics.short: A prepositional phrase hangs under the word it modifies: the preposition on a slanted line, its object on a flat line.
topics.trouble: Learners hang the phrase under the nearest word instead of the word it modifies.

topics.title: Diagrams: Compound Parts and Sentences
topics.short: Compound subjects, verbs and objects split into parallel lines joined by a dashed line with the conjunction. A compound sentence stacks two baselines.
topics.trouble: Learners put the conjunction on the baseline, or draw one baseline for a compound sentence.

topics.title: Diagrams: Appositives and Words Apart
topics.short: An appositive goes in parentheses beside the noun it renames. Interjections and nouns of direct address sit on short lines above the baseline.
topics.trouble: Learners hang an appositive under the noun as if it were an adjective.

topics.title: Diagrams: Participles, Gerunds and Infinitives
topics.short: A participle bends along a curved line under the noun it modifies. A gerund rides a stepped line and an infinitive a bent line (to on the slant); used as nouns, each stands on a forked stand in a noun’s place.
topics.trouble: Learners put verbals on the baseline as if they were the main verb.

topics.title: Diagrams: Adjective and Adverb Clauses
topics.short: A dependent clause gets its own baseline below. A dotted line joins an adjective clause to its noun at the relative pronoun; an adverb clause hangs from the word it modifies, with the conjunction on the dotted line.
topics.trouble: Learners attach the clause to the wrong word, or leave the relative pronoun off the clause’s baseline when it is the clause’s subject or object.

topics.title: Diagrams: Noun Clauses
topics.short: A noun clause sits on a stand in the place a noun would go: subject, direct object or object of a preposition.
topics.trouble: Learners attach a noun clause with a dotted line as if it were a modifier.
